raw_case_text:
We report a case of a 55-year-old man with a de novo congenital STAT1 gain-of-function mutation (c963A>T, p.R321S), as previously reported and validated ( Figure 1A ). The patient presented with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) ( Figure 1B ), complicated by esophageal stenosis, respiratory infections, and bronchiectasis. He received continuous oral antimycotics since childhood, resulting in transient resistance to ketoconazole, fluconazole and itraconazole ( Supplementary E1 ). Genetic and molecular diagnosis ( Figure 1C ) of STAT1 GOF was established at an age of 48 years.
The patient displayed stable respiratory dysfunction. Pulmonary evaluation ( Supplementary E2 ) revealed a progressive obstructive pattern and mild diffusion defect. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed bilateral bronchiectasis. Remarkably, high-sensitivity cardiac troponins were elevated on a routine blood sampling at the age of 49, during a hospital admission for infectious enteritis (0.038 mcg/L, reference <= 0.013,  Supplementary E2 ). No prior measurements were available, yet elevated troponins persisted. The patient did not report thoracic pain or other symptoms suggestive of ischemic heart disease or congestive heart failure. Blood pressure and jugular venous pressure were normal. No peripheral edema was noted. Electrocardiogram ( Figure 2A ) showed a pattern suggestive of right ventricular hypertrophy, biatrial enlargement and biphasic T waves in lateral leads V5-6. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed biventricular concentric hypertrophy and mild diastolic dysfunction with increased left ventricular pressures. Cardiac MRI confirmed these findings, with increased native T1 and T2 values and enhancement of the subepicardial myocardium in the middle and apical zone of the left ventricle on late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), suggesting diffuse myocarditis ( Figure 2B ). Holter monitoring, performed in the context of two (pre)syncopal events, showed frequent ventricular extrasystoles and rare runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT). Ischemic etiology was deemed unlikely based on CT imaging showing absence of coronary stenotic lesions. There were no clinical or radiological arguments for (chronic) pulmonary embolism as a cause of elevated right ventricular pressure. Also, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy was considered unlikely. Whole exome sequencing for congenital cardiomyopathy was not performed.
There were no arguments for invasive fungal infection based on repeated serum blood cultures, beta-D-glucan and aspergillus antigen measurements ( Supplementary E2 ). PCR analysis on blood for common cardiotropic virus, including cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Parvovirus B19 and human herpesvirus-6 and -8 was negative rendering chronic infectious myocarditis improbable. Serology or PCR for other viral origins (enteroviral, adenoviral, human herpesvirus-7 or through microbial cell-free DNA analysis) was not accomplished. Negative autoimmune serology ( Supplementary E2 ), together with the absence of other clinical or biochemical criteria, argued against myocarditis in the context of well-defined autoimmune diseases, although STAT1 GOF is associated with an increased likelihood for autoimmunity. Finally, drug-induced or hypersensitivity myocarditis was deemed improbable. Therefore, the tentative diagnosis of idiopathic myocarditis with unknown onset, presumably immune-mediated in the context of STAT1 GOF was made. No endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) was performed, considering the inherent risk of the procedure and the low probability of chronic viral induced myocarditis. Cardiac transplantation or an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was refused after a multidisciplinary consult. During follow-up, left ventricular function decreased to a nadir left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 41% on TTE and 30% on MRI ( Supplementary E2 ), with persistently active myocarditis on cardiac MRI. Conventional treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction was initiated, including angiotensin converting enzyme inhibition (perindopril 5 mg QD), diuretic treatment (bumetanide 1 mg QD) and a beta blocker (carvedilol 6.25 mg BID). Initially no clinical deterioration was observed except for one episode of cardiac decompensation triggered by a diverticulitis. Because of active myocarditis with profound effects on systolic function, baricitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, was started at a daily dose of 2 mg. After 3 and 8 months of treatment, partial regression of myocarditis was noted on MRI ( Figure 2B ). The patient reported stable exertional dyspnea and improvement of CMC was noted within 3 months of treatment initiation. During this period, there were no major infectious events or need for additional antibiotic treatment. After 8 months, baricitinib was increased to 4 mg daily, with further reduction of cardiac inflammation on MRI at 15 months. However, myocardial fibrosis already occurred, probably due to longstanding inflammation and resulted in persistent biventricular systolic failure. Unfortunately, shortly thereafter, the patient died from a cardiac arrest precipitated by a witnessed VT. Obduction was not performed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old man with congenital STAT1 gain-of-function mutation and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis presented with stable respiratory dysfunction, two presyncopal/syncopal events, and progressive exertional dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis since childhood complicated by esophageal stenosis, recurrent respiratory infections, and bronchiectasis. Genetic diagnosis of STAT1 gain-of-function mutation was established at age 48. At age 49, persistently elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponins were incidentally detected during an admission for infectious enteritis without chest pain or heart failure symptoms. He subsequently experienced two presyncopal/syncopal events and developed progressive left ventricular systolic dysfunction with stable exertional dyspnea, later complicated by an episode of cardiac decompensation triggered by diverticulitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: De novo congenital STAT1 gain-of-function mutation (c.963A>T, p.R321S) diagnosed at age 48; chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) since childhood; esophageal stenosis; recurrent respiratory infections; bilateral bronchiectasis; infectious enteritis at age 49; diverticulitis. Continuous oral antimycotic therapy since childhood with transient resistance to ketoconazole, fluconazole, and itraconazole.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis lesions, stable exertional dyspnea, and two presyncopal/syncopal episodes; negative for thoracic pain or symptoms of ischemic heart disease.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure and jugular venous pressure were normal, with no peripheral edema. Mucocutaneous candidiasis lesions were present.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood sampling at age 49 showed elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin at 0.038 mcg/L (reference <=0.013 mcg/L), which persisted on follow-up. Pulmonary function testing showed a progressive obstructive pattern and mild diffusion defect. ECG demonstrated right ventricular hypertrophy, biatrial enlargement, and biphasic T waves in lateral leads V5-V6. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) initially showed biventricular concentric hypertrophy and mild diastolic dysfunction with increased left ventricular pressures, with LVEF later declining to a nadir of 41%. Holter monitoring revealed frequent ventricular extrasystoles and rare runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Blood cultures and autoimmune serology were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT showed bilateral bronchiectasis, and coronary CT angiography showed absence of coronary stenotic lesions or chronic pulmonary embolism. Cardiac MRI confirmed biventricular hypertrophy with increased native T1 and T2 values and subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in the middle and apical left ventricle suggestive of diffuse myocarditis, with LVEF declining to 30% during follow-up. Repeated serum beta-D-glucan and Aspergillus antigen measurements were negative. Blood PCR assays for CMV, EBV, Parvovirus B19, HHV-6, and HHV-8 were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Idiopathic (presumed immune-mediated) chronic active myocarditis and biventricular heart failure with reduced ejection fraction in the setting of congenital STAT1 gain-of-function mutation and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis; invasive fungal infection (including aspergillosis), viral myocarditis, coronary artery disease, and pulmonary embolism were ruled out by negative serum Aspergillus antigen, beta-D-glucan, blood cultures, viral PCRs, and CT angiography. Managed with perindopril 5 mg daily, bumetanide 1 mg daily, carvedilol 6.25 mg twice daily, and targeted JAK1/2 inhibition with baricitinib 2 mg daily (increased to 4 mg daily at 8 months), which improved CMC within 3 months and partially regressed myocardial inflammation on MRI at 3, 8, and 15 months; however, established myocardial fibrosis led to persistent biventricular systolic failure and fatal cardiac arrest from witnessed ventricular tachycardia.
